nameStory: The 'Variable Brown Dotlets' name perfectly captures this lichen's most striking feature - tiny brown dots that seem to change their appearance depending on conditions. The scientific name Xanthosyne comes from Greek words meaning 'yellow together,' hinting at the yellowish tones that can appear in the lichen's body when wet or in certain light.
description: Variable Brown Dotlets form thin, crusty patches that hug tightly to rock surfaces like a coat of rough paint. The lichen body itself is typically grayish to brownish, but what really catches your eye are the small, dark brown to black dots scattered across the surface - these are the reproductive structures called apothecia. Individual patches can grow quite large over many years, sometimes reaching 4-6 inches across, though you'll often find smaller colonies just getting started.

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Look for small, dark brown to black dots (apothecia) scattered across the surface like tiny buttons - they're usually about 1-2mm wide and sit flush with or slightly raised above the lichen body

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms a thin, crusty coating that's firmly attached to rock - you can't peel it off like you could with leafy lichens, and it feels rough like fine sandpaper when you run your finger over it

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: The main body ranges from pale gray when dry to brownish-gray when wet, sometimes showing subtle yellowish hints in good light - the contrast makes those dark dots really pop

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost always found on hard rock surfaces, particularly granite and other acidic rocks - rarely if ever on tree bark or softer stones

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The surface feels slightly gritty and has a matte finish rather than being shiny or smooth - somewhat like touching a fine emery board

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual colonies can spread several inches across on suitable rocks, though young patches may be just an inch or two wide - grows very slowly over many years

habitat: Variable Brown Dotlets prefer exposed or semi-shaded granite outcrops, stone walls, and large boulders throughout New England's forests and rocky areas. They're particularly common on acidic rocks in higher elevation areas and can often be found on the same rocks as other crustose lichens. Look for them on vertical or gently sloping rock faces that get some moisture but aren't constantly wet.

seasonality.spring: The lichen body may appear more vibrant after spring rains, with the grayish surface showing more pronounced color variations. This is a good time to spot the contrast between the wet lichen body and the dark reproductive dots.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer weather, the lichen appears more muted and grayish, but the dark apothecia remain prominent and are often easiest to photograph in good light conditions.
seasonality.fall: Fall moisture brings out subtle color changes in the lichen body, and the increased humidity may make the surface feel slightly less gritty to the touch.
seasonality.winter: Snow and ice may cover colonies for extended periods, but when visible, the lichen maintains its appearance year-round - winter is actually great for spotting them on snow-free rock faces.

funFact: Despite their tiny size, the dark dots (apothecia) on Variable Brown Dotlets can live for decades and continue producing spores year after year - some of those little brown buttons you're looking at might be older than you are!
confusionNotes: Variable Brown Dotlets can be confused with other small, dark-dotted crustose lichens on rocks, but most similar species have lighter brown or reddish dots rather than the distinctly dark brown to black apothecia. Remember: if the dots look almost black and the lichen is on hard rock, you're probably looking at Variable Brown Dotlets.
compareHints: Since Variable Brown Dotlets is the only Xanthosyne species commonly found in New England, compare it with other small crustose lichens in the rim lichen family. Most similar species either have different colored apothecia (often lighter brown or reddish), grow on different substrates like tree bark, or lack the distinctive dark dotted appearance that makes this species so recognizable.
